title: Did Scientists Just Spot Dark Matter? One Clue Has Physicists Excited
summary:
Dark matter is an invisible substance that scientists think makes up most of the matter in the universe. They can sense its gravity tugging on stars and other objects in space. But no one knows what it is, and no one has ever directly observed it, despite decades of searching.

Now, a detector called LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, may have glimpsed it for the first time. But scientists say they cannot be sure yet.

LZ is located at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota. It searches for proposed particles called WIMPs, short for weakly interacting massive particles. Some scientists think WIMPs might make up dark matter. If a WIMP crashed into the center, or nucleus, of an atom in LZ's tank of liquid xenon, it would send that nucleus zinging away and give off a tiny flash of light and electrons. Sensors in the detector are designed to spot those signals.

The team combed through 220 days' worth of data, looking for a type of WIMP that would push xenon nuclei away at high energies. They found just one event that fits. It was recorded in June 2023. The team shared its findings on September 1 at a scientific meeting in Japan.

"We got left with one event, which is fascinating. Absolutely fascinating," said Rick Gaitskell, a physicist at Brown University and a spokesperson for LZ.

The team estimates there is only about a 1 in 100 chance that known particles caused the event. Physicists usually need much stronger proof before they say they have found evidence of something new, so more data is needed.

Wick Haxton, a physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not part of the research, called it "the most interesting thing that's come up in recent times."
why_it_matters: Finding dark matter would help explain what most of the matter in the universe is made of. The story also shows how scientists wait for strong proof before announcing a discovery.

background_read: Dark matter is the name scientists give to unseen material whose gravity seems to help hold galaxies together and affect how stars move.
Because it does not give off or reflect light, scientists try to catch it in other ways, such as watching for rare bumps between dark matter particles and ordinary atoms.
Detectors for these searches are often built deep underground, where layers of rock block many other particles that could cause false signals.
WIMPs are one popular idea for what dark matter particles might be.
